blocks.text: A first-order, first degree differential equation is called Homogeneous if it can be written in the form

blocks.text_alt: d y by d x equals F of y over x

blocks.text: where \(F\left(\frac{y}{x}\right)\) is a function of the ratio \(\frac{y}{x}\) only. For example, \(\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{x^3 + xy^2}{y^3 - x^2y}\) is a homogeneous differential equation because, it can be written as:
On the other hand, the differential equation \(\frac{dy}{dx} = x + y\) is not homogeneous because \(x + y\) cannot be expressed as a function of \(\frac{y}{x}\).

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
A quick test for fractions: if every term of the numerator and of the denominator has the same degree \(n\), divide top and bottom by \(x^n\); every term then turns into a power of \(\frac{y}{x}\). In the example, \(x^3\), \(xy^2\), \(y^3\), \(x^2y\) all have degree 3, so we divide by \(x^3\).
Why \(x + y\) fails: \(x + y = x\left(1 + \frac{y}{x}\right)\) always leaves an \(x\) outside. A homogeneous right side must not change when \(x\) and \(y\) are both multiplied by the same number \(t\): \(\frac{tx + ty}{ty - tx} = \frac{x + y}{y - x}\), but \(tx + ty \ne x + y\).
Method to Solve a Homogeneous Differential Equation

The homogeneous differential equation:
\[\dfrac{dy}{dx} = F\left(\dfrac{y}{x}\right) \quad \text{...(1)}\]
can be converted into a separable differential equation in variables \(x\) and \(v\) by making the substitution:
\[y = vx \quad \text{...(2)}\]

Differentiating both sides of equation (2) w.r.t \(x\):
\[\dfrac{dy}{dx} = v + x\dfrac{dv}{dx} \quad \text{...(3)}\]

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Where (3) comes from: \(v\) is not a constant, it is a new unknown function of \(x\) (\(v = \frac{y}{x}\)). So \(y = v \cdot x\) is a product and we use the product rule:
\[\dfrac{dy}{dx} = v \cdot 1 + x\dfrac{dv}{dx}\]
Writing \(\frac{dy}{dx} = v\) (forgetting the second term) is the most common error in this topic.

Substituting the values of \(\frac{y}{x}\) and \(\frac{dy}{dx}\) from equations (2) and (3), the equation (1) can be written as:
\[v + x\dfrac{dv}{dx} = F(v)\]
Rewriting, we obtain:
\[x\dfrac{dv}{dx} = F(v) - v\]

It becomes separable differential equation.
\[\dfrac{1}{F(v) - v}\,dv = \dfrac{1}{x}\,dx\]
On integrating both sides:
\[\int \dfrac{1}{F(v) - v}\,dv = \int \dfrac{1}{x}\,dx\]
By solving integrals of the above equation and then substituting back \(v = \frac{y}{x}\), we obtain the general solution for the homogeneous differential equation (1).

blocks.title: Note
blocks.text: If the equation \(\frac{dy}{dx} = f(x, y)\) is homogeneous, then on substituting \(y = vx\), \(\frac{dy}{dx}\) is replaced by \(v + x\frac{dv}{dx}\) and \(f(x, y)\) can easily be simplified by replacing \(x\) with 1 and \(y\) with \(v\). For example, in \(\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{x + y}{y - x}\), replacing \(x\) with 1 and \(y\) with \(v\) in the right-hand side, we get \(v + x\frac{dv}{dx} = \frac{1 + v}{v - 1}\).

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Why the shortcut in the Note works: put \(y = vx\) in \(f\); every term has the same degree, so a power of \(x\) comes out of the top and bottom and cancels:
\[\dfrac{x + vx}{vx - x} = \dfrac{x(1 + v)}{x(v - 1)} = \dfrac{1 + v}{v - 1}\]
The result is exactly what you get by writing 1 for \(x\) and \(v\) for \(y\).

blocks.title: Numbering note (ours)
blocks.text: The book prints these two examples as "Example 4" and "Example 5" (its numbering restarted at Example 2 in 4.2.1, so "Example 4" is printed twice in this unit). We show them as Example 7 and Example 8, continuing the unit's sequence.

blocks.title: Example 7
blocks.problem: Find the general solution of the differential equation \(\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{x + y}{y - x}\).
steps:
Given: \(\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{x + y}{y - x}\) ...(1)
To find: the general solution.
Method: every term of the numerator and denominator of \(f(x, y) = \frac{x + y}{y - x}\) is of degree 1, so (1) is homogeneous. Put \(y = vx\), \(\frac{dy}{dx} = v + x\frac{dv}{dx}\), separate \(v\) and \(x\), integrate, then put back \(v = \frac{y}{x}\).

Step 1: Substitute \(y = vx\)
\[v + x\dfrac{dv}{dx} = \dfrac{x + vx}{vx - x}\]
\[= \dfrac{1 + v}{v - 1}\]
Why: cancel the common factor \(x\) (this is the Note: replace \(x\) by 1 and \(y\) by \(v\)).

Step 2: Isolate \(x\frac{dv}{dx}\)
\[x\dfrac{dv}{dx} = \dfrac{1 + v}{v - 1} - v\]
\[= \dfrac{1 + v - v^2 + v}{v - 1}\]
\[= \dfrac{-v^2 + 2v + 1}{v - 1}\]
Why: subtract \(v\) from both sides and use the common denominator \(v - 1\).

Step 3: Separate \(v\) and \(x\)
\[\dfrac{v - 1}{-v^2 + 2v + 1}\,dv = \dfrac{1}{x}\,dx\]
Why: now only \(v\) is on the left and only \(x\) on the right; the equation is separable.

Step 4: Make the numerator the derivative of the denominator
\[\dfrac{d}{dv}(-v^2 + 2v + 1) = -2v + 2\]
\[v - 1 = -\dfrac{1}{2}(-2v + 2)\]
So
\[-\dfrac{1}{2}\int \dfrac{-2v + 2}{-v^2 + 2v + 1}\,dv\]
\[= \ln|x| + \ln|c|\]
Why: then \(\int \frac{f'(v)}{f(v)}\,dv = \ln|f(v)|\). Writing the constant as \(\ln|c|\) lets the logarithms combine.

Step 5: Integrate and combine the logarithms
\[-\dfrac{1}{2}\ln|-v^2 + 2v + 1| = \ln|cx|\]
\[\ln|-v^2 + 2v + 1| = -2\ln|cx|\]
\[= \ln|cx|^{-2}\]
Why: \(\ln|x| + \ln|c| = \ln|cx|\); multiply by \(-2\); \(k\ln a = \ln a^k\).

Step 6: Remove the logarithms
\[|-v^2 + 2v + 1| = \dfrac{1}{c^2x^2}\]
Why: if \(\ln A = \ln B\) then \(A = B\); and \(|cx|^{-2} = \frac{1}{c^2x^2}\).

Step 7: Substitute \(v = \frac{y}{x}\) back
\[\left|-\dfrac{y^2}{x^2} + \dfrac{2y}{x} + 1\right| = \dfrac{1}{c^2x^2}\]
\[\dfrac{|-y^2 + 2xy + x^2|}{x^2} = \dfrac{1}{c^2x^2}\]
\[|-y^2 + 2xy + x^2| = \dfrac{1}{c^2}\]
\[-y^2 + 2xy + x^2 = \pm\dfrac{1}{c^2}\]
Why: take the common denominator \(x^2\), then multiply both sides by \(x^2\). Removing the absolute value gives \(\pm\).

Step 8: Rename the constant
\(\pm\frac{1}{c^2}\) is just a non-zero constant; call it \(c\) (\(c \ne 0\)):
\[-y^2 + 2xy + x^2 = c\]
\[x^2 + 2xy - y^2 = c\]
Why: the constant is arbitrary, so any non-zero constant expression may be called \(c\).

Check:
Differentiate \(x^2 + 2xy - y^2 = c\):
\[2x + 2y + 2x\dfrac{dy}{dx} - 2y\dfrac{dy}{dx} = 0\]
\[(y - x)\dfrac{dy}{dx} = x + y\]
\[\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac{x + y}{y - x}\]
This is equation (1).

blocks.title: Example 8
steps:
Given: \(x\sin\left(\frac{y}{x}\right)dy - \left[y\sin\left(\frac{y}{x}\right) - x\right]dx = 0\).
To find: the general solution.
Method: write it as \(\frac{dy}{dx} = \ldots\); dividing through by \(x\) shows the right side depends on \(\frac{y}{x}\) only, so it is homogeneous. Then put \(y = vx\).

Step 1: Rewrite as \(\frac{dy}{dx}\)
\[\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac{y\sin\left(\frac{y}{x}\right) - x}{x\sin\left(\frac{y}{x}\right)}\]
\[= \dfrac{\frac{y}{x}\sin\left(\frac{y}{x}\right) - 1}{\sin\left(\frac{y}{x}\right)}\]
Why: move the \(dx\) term across, divide by \(x\sin\frac{y}{x}\,dx\); then divide top and bottom by \(x\).

Step 2: Recognise the type
The right side is a function of \(\frac{y}{x}\) only, so the equation is homogeneous. Put \(y = vx\):
\[v + x\dfrac{dv}{dx} = \dfrac{v\sin v - 1}{\sin v}\]
Why: \(\frac{y}{x} = v\) and \(\frac{dy}{dx} = v + x\frac{dv}{dx}\).

Step 3: Isolate \(x\frac{dv}{dx}\)
\[x\dfrac{dv}{dx} = \dfrac{v\sin v - 1}{\sin v} - v\]
\[= \dfrac{v\sin v - 1 - v\sin v}{\sin v}\]
\[= -\dfrac{1}{\sin v}\]
Why: subtract \(v = \frac{v\sin v}{\sin v}\); the \(v\sin v\) terms cancel.

Step 4: Separate \(v\) and \(x\)
\[-\sin v\,dv = \dfrac{1}{x}\,dx\]
Why: multiply both sides by \(-\sin v\) and by \(\frac{dx}{x}\).

Step 5: Integrate both sides
\[\int (-\sin v)\,dv = \int \dfrac{1}{x}\,dx\]
\[\cos v = \ln|x| + \ln|c|\]
Why: \(\int(-\sin v)\,dv = \cos v\) because \(\frac{d}{dv}\cos v = -\sin v\); \(\int\frac{dx}{x} = \ln|x|\); constant written as \(\ln|c|\).

Step 6: Put \(v = \frac{y}{x}\) back
\[\cos\left(\dfrac{y}{x}\right) = \ln|cx|\]
Why: \(\ln|x| + \ln|c| = \ln|cx|\), and the answer must be in \(x\) and \(y\).

Check:
Differentiate \(\cos\frac{y}{x} = \ln|cx|\):
\[-\sin\dfrac{y}{x} \cdot \dfrac{x\frac{dy}{dx} - y}{x^2} = \dfrac{1}{x}\]
Multiply by \(-x^2\):
\[\sin\dfrac{y}{x}\left(x\dfrac{dy}{dx} - y\right) = -x\]
\[x\sin\dfrac{y}{x}\,dy - \left[y\sin\dfrac{y}{x} - x\right]dx = 0\]
which is the given equation.

rows: Right side depends on the ratio \(\frac{y}{x}\) only (all terms of the same degree)
blocks.caption: Separable vs homogeneous (our teaching summary)

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. Homogeneous means \(\frac{dy}{dx} = F\left(\frac{y}{x}\right)\); for a fraction, every term of the top and bottom has the same degree.
2. Substitute \(y = vx\) and \(\frac{dy}{dx} = v + x\frac{dv}{dx}\) (product rule).
3. Shortcut: in \(f(x, y)\) write 1 for \(x\) and \(v\) for \(y\).
4. Then \(x\frac{dv}{dx} = F(v) - v\) is separable: \(\frac{dv}{F(v) - v} = \frac{dx}{x}\).
5. Write the constant as \(\ln|c|\) when the other terms are logarithms; at the end put \(v = \frac{y}{x}\) back.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
1. Writing \(\frac{dy}{dx} = v\) instead of \(v + x\frac{dv}{dx}\).
2. Forgetting to subtract \(v\): the separable form is \(x\frac{dv}{dx} = F(v) - v\), not \(F(v)\).
3. Leaving the answer in \(v\); the final answer must be in \(x\) and \(y\).
4. Calling \(x + y\) or \(e^{x - y}\) homogeneous: their terms do not all have the same degree.
